title: SQL with sqlite3: asking a database questions
summary: Create tables, insert rows safely with placeholders, and ask questions with SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and joins, using the sqlite3 module.

sources.section: sqlite3 — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases
How to use placeholders to bind values in SQL queries

steps.title: Questions about a lot of data
steps.body:
Which customers spent most this month? Which team scored the most points? With a few rows you can loop over a
list of dicts. With a hundred thousand rows, kept on disk between runs and shared by programs, you want a
**database**: you describe the answer you want in **SQL**, and the database finds it. Python comes with
`sqlite3`, a complete database in a single file (or in memory) with no server to set up.

steps.title: Tables of rows, and questions about them
steps.body:
A database holds **tables**, like spreadsheets with named, typed columns: `books (title TEXT, year
INTEGER)`. You don't loop over the rows yourself. You ask a question in SQL, such as `SELECT title FROM
books WHERE year > 1900 ORDER BY year`, and get back rows as Python tuples.

One rule matters more than any other: never paste values into the SQL text yourself. Put a `?` where each
value goes and pass the values separately. Then a name like `O'Brien`, or text that happens to look like
SQL, is stored as plain data instead of changing your query.

questions: What could go wrong if a user's name were pasted straight into the SQL text?
Why ask the database to sort and count instead of doing it in a Python loop?

steps.title: Watch a row go in and come back out
steps.body: Each `execute` sends one SQL statement to the database; a SELECT comes back as rows. Each frame shows the variables just before the highlighted line runs; a frame with output shows what its line printed.

visual.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE pets (name TEXT, age INTEGER)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO pets VALUES (?, ?)", ("Rex", 3))
row = con.execute("SELECT name, age FROM pets").fetchone()
print(row)

frames.note: Open a database. ":memory:" keeps it in memory; a file name would keep it on disk.
Create a table with two typed columns.
Insert one row. The two `?` are filled from the tuple, safely.
Ask for the rows; `fetchone()` takes the first, as a tuple.
Rows come back as plain tuples.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Connecting:** `con = sqlite3.connect("file.db")` opens (or creates) a database file; `":memory:"` makes
a temporary one. `con.execute(sql, params)` runs one statement and returns a cursor; `executemany` runs it
once per item of a list of tuples. Changes to a file are saved by `con.commit()`; `con.close()` closes it.

**Tables:** `CREATE TABLE name (column TYPE, ...)` with types such as `TEXT`, `INTEGER` and `REAL`.
`INSERT INTO name VALUES (?, ?)` adds a row.

**Queries:** `SELECT columns FROM table`, then optionally `WHERE condition`, `GROUP BY column` (one row per
group, with `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(x)`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `AVG`), `ORDER BY column [DESC], ...` and `LIMIT n`. A
cursor can be looped over, or read with `fetchone()` (a tuple, or `None` if there are no more rows) and
`fetchall()` (a list of tuples).

**Placeholders:** each `?` in the SQL takes the next value from the parameters tuple; a single value
still needs a tuple, `(n,)`. Never build SQL with f-strings or `+` from values.

**Joins:** `FROM a JOIN b ON a.key = b.key` pairs matching rows; `LEFT JOIN` also keeps rows of `a` with no
match, filling `b`'s columns with `NULL` (`None` in Python). `COALESCE(x, 0)` turns a `NULL` into 0.

steps.title: Run it: create, insert, ask
steps.body:
A filtered, sorted query; a count and a minimum in one row; and a title full of SQL-looking text that a
placeholder treats as an ordinary (unmatched) string.
steps.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE books (title TEXT, year INTEGER)")
con.executemany("INSERT INTO books VALUES (?, ?)", [("Dune", 1965), ("Neuromancer", 1984), ("Emma", 1815)])

for row in con.execute("SELECT title, year FROM books WHERE year > ? ORDER BY year", (1900,)):
    print(row)

print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*), MIN(year) FROM books").fetchone())

name = "Emma'; DROP TABLE books; --"
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE title = ?", (name,)).fetchone())
con.close()

steps.title: Your turn: safe inserts and a top-n query
steps.body:
`setup(con)` creates a `scores` table. Fix `add_score(con, name, points)`, which builds its SQL with an
f-string and breaks on a name like `O'Brien`, so that it uses placeholders. Then write `top(con, n)`: the `n`
highest scores as a list of `(name, points)` tuples, highest first, ties in alphabetical order of name.
hints: `ORDER BY points DESC, name LIMIT ?`, with `(n,)` as the parameters, then `.fetchall()`.

tests.name: highest first, ties by name
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
setup(con)
for row in [('cy', 4), ('ben', 9), ('ana', 9), ('dee', 1)]:
    add_score(con, *row)
assert top(con, 3) == [('ana', 9), ('ben', 9), ('cy', 4)], top(con, 3)

tests.name: n can be 0, or more than there are rows
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
setup(con)
add_score(con, 'ana', 2)
assert top(con, 0) == []
assert top(con, 5) == [('ana', 2)]

tests.name: names with quotes of either kind are stored as they are
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
setup(con)
names = ["O'Brien", 'say "hi"', 'both \' and "']
for k, n in enumerate(names):
    add_score(con, n, 10 - k)
assert top(con, 3) == [(n, 10 - k) for k, n in enumerate(names)], top(con, 3)

tests.name: the name is passed as a parameter, not inside the SQL
SQL-looking text is just data
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
setup(con)
name = "x', 0); DROP TABLE scores; --"
add_score(con, name, 3)
add_score(con, 'ana', 5)
assert top(con, 2) == [('ana', 5), (name, 3)], 'the name should be stored as plain text and the table should still exist'

tests.name: the table holds what was added
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
setup(con)
add_score(con, 'ana', 2)
add_score(con, 'ben', 3)
assert con.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scores').fetchone() == (2,)

steps.title: Challenge: totals per team
steps.body:
The database has `players (name, team)` and `scores (name, points)`, where a player can have many scores
or none. Write `team_totals(con)`: one `(team, total)` tuple for every team that has players, where `total` is
the sum of its players' points (0 if they have none), highest total first, ties in alphabetical order of team.
Scores for names that aren't players don't count.
steps.starter:
def team_totals(con):
    return con.execute("SELECT team, 0 FROM players").fetchall()
hints: Start from `players` and `LEFT JOIN scores` on the name, so teams without scores are kept.
`GROUP BY` the team, `COALESCE(SUM(points), 0)` for the total, then `ORDER BY total DESC, team`.

tests.name: sums each team's scores
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE players (name TEXT, team TEXT)')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE scores (name TEXT, points INTEGER)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO players VALUES (?, ?)', [('ana', 'red'), ('ben', 'red'), ('cy', 'blue')])
con.executemany('INSERT INTO scores VALUES (?, ?)', [('ana', 3), ('ana', 4), ('ben', 1), ('cy', 5)])
assert team_totals(con) == [('red', 8), ('blue', 5)], team_totals(con)

tests.name: a team with no scores has total 0
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE players (name TEXT, team TEXT)')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE scores (name TEXT, points INTEGER)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO players VALUES (?, ?)', [('ana', 'red'), ('dee', 'green')])
con.execute('INSERT INTO scores VALUES (?, ?)', ('ana', 2))
assert team_totals(con) == [('red', 2), ('green', 0)], team_totals(con)

tests.name: ties are in alphabetical order of team
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE players (name TEXT, team TEXT)')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE scores (name TEXT, points INTEGER)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO players VALUES (?, ?)', [('a', 'zeta'), ('b', 'alpha')])
con.executemany('INSERT INTO scores VALUES (?, ?)', [('a', 4), ('b', 4)])
assert team_totals(con) == [('alpha', 4), ('zeta', 4)], team_totals(con)

tests.name: scores for non-players don't count
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE players (name TEXT, team TEXT)')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE scores (name TEXT, points INTEGER)')
con.execute('INSERT INTO players VALUES (?, ?)', ('ana', 'red'))
con.executemany('INSERT INTO scores VALUES (?, ?)', [('ana', 1), ('ghost', 99)])
assert team_totals(con) == [('red', 1)], team_totals(con)

tests.name: no players, no rows
tests.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE players (name TEXT, team TEXT)')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE scores (name TEXT, points INTEGER)')
assert team_totals(con) == []

questions.prompt: A table `pets` has rows ('Rex', 3), ('Ada', 1) and ('Bo', 5). What does `SELECT name FROM pets WHERE age > 2 ORDER BY name` return?
questions.explanation: WHERE keeps Rex and Bo; ORDER BY name sorts them alphabetically.

questions.prompt: Why pass values as parameters (`?`) instead of putting them into the SQL with an f-string?
choices: The values are sent separately, so quotes or SQL inside them can't change the query
It is the only way to insert numbers
sqlite3 doesn't accept strings in SQL
questions.explanation: With placeholders the database never reads your data as SQL: no broken quotes, no injection.

questions.prompt: What does `con.execute("SELECT * FROM pets WHERE age > 99").fetchone()` return when no row matches?
questions.explanation: `fetchone()` returns the next row, or `None` when there are no rows left.

questions.prompt: `players LEFT JOIN scores ON ...`: what happens to a player with no scores?
choices: The player is kept, with NULL (None) for the score columns
The player gets a score of 0 automatically
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; COALESCE can then turn NULL into 0.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Open a database with `sqlite3.connect`, create tables and insert rows.
- Always pass values with `?` placeholders, never by building SQL text.
- Ask questions with SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT and GROUP BY, and read rows as tuples.
- Combine tables with JOIN and LEFT JOIN, using COALESCE for missing values.
